title: Why You Need To Stay The Course With Difficult Students
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin criticizes the common pattern of cycling difficult students through rewards, lectures, behavior contracts, and punishments in rapid, inconsistent succession, arguing this constant tightening and loosening confuses students and virtually guarantees their behavior never truly changes. His alternative is patient, unwavering consistency — the same calm, steady progression of consequences applied day after day, week after week, without shortcuts, flattery, or ignored misbehavior. He argues that real change in difficult students comes only when they can no longer blame others and are forced to confront that they themselves are the problem, a process he compares to the slow turn of an oil tanker rather than a sudden breakthrough. This requires the teacher to trust the process even when no visible improvement appears at first, and to treat the most difficult students with the same dignity and good humor extended to the best-behaved ones, rather than resorting to degrading rewards or fake praise.
points: Cycling difficult students rapidly between rewards, lectures, and punishments confuses them and virtually guarantees their behavior never truly changes.
Lasting change in difficult students requires patient, unwavering consistency applied over a long period, not quick fixes or shortcuts.
Real behavioral change happens only when students can no longer blame others and are forced to confront that they are the problem.
Teachers should avoid degrading rewards, prize boxes, and fake praise, and instead praise only what is genuinely earned.
Difficult students should be treated with the same dignity and good humor extended to the best-behaved students in the class.
quotes: Difficult students are treated like temperamental orchids, forever subject to trial and error. What works for awhile never seems to last, so let’s try something else.
It’s to stay the course. It’s to be the same steady, calm, and kind teacher who follows the same progression of consequences day after day and week after week.
You see, with your most challenging students, improvement doesn’t happen overnight. It takes time. A slow turn of an oil tanker.
You do what is best for them long term by relying on the natural law that we learn when lessons come from realizing our own mistakes.
You must believe in them and have the toughness to say no to degrading tokens, prize boxes, rewards, and fake praise.
Treat your toughest students with the same dignity and good humor as your very best.
